newsitem.title: USA: Bombay Co. furniture goes back to roots.
newsitem.headline: Bombay Co. furniture goes back to roots.

text.p: Cutting short a costly flirtation with young and trendy customers, the Bombay Company will refocus on the lower-priced antique reproduction furniture it made its name with, new Chief Executive Officer Carson Thompson said.

One week after ousting former Wall Street darlings Robert and Alexandra Nourse from the management team, Thompson said getting back to basics is central to the Fort Worth-based furniture retailer's turnaround bid.

He said the Nourses had tried to go "too upscale, too fashionable" with an eclectic line of light woods and metals, and neglected to bring in new models for its traditional line of mahogany, cherry and other darkwood desks and tables.
"To a significant extent they just vacated our mainstream business that is an extremely important part of the company," Thompson said in an interview.
"What we are doing here now is refocusing on the core Bombay business with the known strategies that have worked historically."
That means turning back towards Bombay's core customers: women in their 40's, with children and a household income in the region of $70,000.

Bombay's sales and profits soared in the early 1990s and, with the Nourse husband-and-wife team winning glowing tributes from industry analysts, its stock jumped to well over $30 a share in early 1994.
Since then, however, profit margins have shrunk and the share price has plummeted back down to around $6.
Thompson said the collapse was easily explained.

An inadequate number of new products meant the company had to offer "excessive" promotional sales in order to keep revenues coming in. That hurt margins and shortened the life-cycle of product lines, exacerbating the problem of new models.
Rescuing the company, he said, will take a year or more.

"It is going to take us five months to re-position our inventory and it takes usually at least six months to get a new product stream started. And it takes beyond that then to get completely on track," said Thompson. "This is not a few-day turnaround."
In the six months ended Aug. 3, Bombay's chain of 431 stores posted a net loss of $4.8 million, or 12 cents a share, on lower revenues of $139 million.
Thompson said the company would also lose money in the third quarter, would rebound briefly during the Christmas season and then post losses again in the first half of 1997.

He was optimistic that, once new lines are introduced for Bombay's traditional customers, it will be able to reduce promotional sales, restore margins and post steady profits in the last six months of 1997 and beyond.
He said Bombay was currently testing two pilot stores in outlet malls and over the next nine to 15 months will consider opening stores abroad, notably in Japan, Britain and France.
